title: Clifton Wells: Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Clifton wells have a 20 ft median depth, but yields are highly variable. Typical completed well cost: $7,000-$13,500.
h1: What Clifton, Colorado Wells Are Really Like
intro_html:
Well records within 5 miles of Clifton show a shallow but highly variable local groundwater picture. Among 691 permitted wells, the median reported depth is 20 feet, and the middle half runs from 15 to 30 feet. That does not mean every lot has easy water. Most records are monitoring wells, not household wells, and only 25 wells report a pump yield.

For a buyer, the useful starting point is the nearby well map, not a countywide average. Fruitvale, Orchard Mesa, Grand Junction, Palisade, Redlands and Fruita can provide context, but the neighboring parcels closest to a property usually matter most.

sections.heading: Clifton well depth: shallow records, unusual deep holes
sections.html:
Clifton’s recorded wells are generally shallow. Ninety-three percent are under 100 feet, while 4% fall from 100 to 300 feet, 1% from 300 to 600 feet, and 2% are deeper than 600 feet. The deepest recorded well reaches 4,629 feet, so the range is not something a contractor should ignore.

The 20-foot median and 15-to-30-foot middle half can help frame a bid for a simple shallow hole, but they are not a guarantee for a domestic well. The aquifer designation is unnamed or fractured-bedrock for 626 wells, while 37 are listed as alluvial and one as Mancos. Ground conditions, the exact lot, casing and grout requirements, and the intended use will control the final design.

sections.heading: How much water can a Clifton well produce?
sections.html:
Reported yield is the biggest caution in these records. The median is 0.1 gallons per minute, with a middle half from 0.1 to 13.0 gallons per minute. Sixty-eight percent of reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute, 8% produce from 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 24% report more than 15 gallons per minute. No wells are shown in the 1-to-5 gallon-per-minute category.

Those figures come from only 25 yield reports, so they describe recorded results rather than every Clifton well. A buyer should ask for the well permit, construction report, pump test and storage setup. A low-producing well may still work with adequate tank storage, but it can be a poor fit for irrigation, livestock or a larger home.

sections.heading: Clifton water levels and the change by decade
sections.html:
The median static water level is 10 feet below ground, with the middle half between 8 and 28 feet. That is a shallow water level in the available records, but only 31 wells report one. Measurements also vary with location, season, well construction and the date of measurement.

The decade comparison deserves attention: the median reported level was 5 feet below ground in the 2000s and 27 feet below ground in the 2020s. That pattern is consistent with deeper measured water levels in the later records, but it does not prove a basin-wide decline because the wells and measurement conditions may differ. Before buying, compare nearby logs and ask for recent measurements from the specific property.

sections.heading: Who has drilled near Clifton, and when?
sections.html:
Permit activity has been uneven over time. The records show 2 permits in the 1950s, 1 in the 1960s, 8 in the 1970s, 48 in the 1980s, 147 in the 1990s, 114 in the 2000s, 182 in the 2010s and 80 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2024.

Authorized (Pe, Pg) is the most common driller entry, with 240 records. Owner appears on 7, and Terracon Consultants Inc. (Rogers, Richard C.) appears on 6. These entries are useful leads, not a recommendation or proof that any driller is available for a new job. Check the Colorado Division of Water Resources permit and construction records, then verify current licensing, insurance and experience with the ground on your lot.

sections.heading: What a new Clifton well may cost
sections.html:
The local cost model assumes mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. A typical drilling rate is $50 to $75 per foot. At the 20-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone models to about $1,000 to $1,500.

That is not the price of a functioning water system. A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $7,000 to $13,500. A deeper-than-typical hole, difficult access, extra casing or grout, water testing, storage, treatment and connection work can change the proposal. Ask each bidder to separate drilling, casing, grouting, pump equipment, trenching, electrical and testing so the low bid is not simply missing part of the system.

sections.heading: Clifton risks to check before you build
sections.html:
Low yield is the clearest recorded risk: 68% of reported yields are under 1 gallon per minute. Dry holes and poor production are possible in fractured-bedrock settings because a productive fracture may not be predictable from the surface. A driller should review nearby logs and explain what happens if the hole does not meet the intended use.

Water quality also needs site-specific testing. Within about 10 miles are 63 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 37 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites and 17 historic mine features. Their presence does not establish contamination on a particular parcel, but it supports testing before closing and again before occupancy. Confirm septic setbacks, building envelopes, access for a rig, and the location of casing and grout before finalizing a home plan.

sections.heading: A practical plan for a Clifton lot
sections.html:
Start with the closest permitted wells in Clifton, then compare records from Fruitvale and Orchard Mesa where the geology and development pattern may offer useful context. Give the driller the parcel, proposed house location, septic area and access route before requesting a firm estimate. A well permit from the Colorado Division of Water Resources is not the same thing as a guarantee of water quality or production.

For a household well, confirm the permitted use and any augmentation-plan requirements that apply to the water right. Do not assume a monitoring well can serve a home. Before closing, obtain the construction report, yield information, water-level history and laboratory water test when available. For a new build, coordinate the well, septic system, driveway, electrical route and storage tank so one installation does not block another.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Clifton, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded depth within 5 miles of Clifton is 20 feet, and the middle half runs from 15 to 30 feet. Ninety-three percent of recorded wells are under 100 feet. The range is still wide: the deepest record is 4,629 feet, so nearby well logs are more useful than the median alone.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Clifton?
faq.a: The local model uses $50 to $75 per foot. At the 20-foot median depth, drilling the hole is estimated at about $1,000 to $1,500. A completed system with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at $7,000 to $13,500. Access, casing, grout, testing and unusual depth can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water does a Clifton well produce?
faq.a: Reported production is very uneven. The median yield is 0.1 gallons per minute, and 68% of reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute. The middle half ranges from 0.1 to 13.0 gallons per minute. Only 25 wells report a yield, so obtain the specific property’s pump test and plan for storage if production is low.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Clifton, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from the well map alone. Within about 10 miles are 63 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 37 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites and 17 historic mine features. Those locations do not prove a parcel is affected. Test the actual well through a qualified laboratory before drinking and review nearby land uses and records.

faq.q: Are Clifton water levels getting lower?
faq.a: The reported median static water level was 5 feet below ground in the 2000s and 27 feet below ground in the 2020s. That indicates deeper measured water levels in the later decade, but only 31 wells report static levels and the wells may differ. Treat it as a reason to investigate, not proof of a uniform decline across Clifton.
